title: BUG: numpy.any returns True given a boolean array of all False with the intel compiler
body: I installed NumPy 1.26.2 on an x86_64 Linux HPC system. For a one-dimensional boolean array containing only False, np.any returns False at length 63 but True at length 64 or greater. Python 3.11.6 reports a GCC Intel C++ 11.3.1 mode build. The runtime information reports Intel MKL 2023.1 and support for AVX512_SKX among the detected SIMD extensions. This operation has returned False across the other NumPy versions and platforms I have used, and I rely on it regularly for filtering data.

symptoms_visible: With NumPy 1.26.2, np.any(np.zeros(63, bool)) prints False, but np.any(np.zeros(64, bool)) prints True even though every element is False.
N0.label: N0 incorrect boolean reduction reported

symptoms_visible: My source-built Intel-compiler NumPy returns True for an all-False array at length 64 or greater in its normal configuration.
When I set NPY_DISABLE_CPU_FEATURES="AVX512_SKX", np.any returns False for all-False arrays, including lengths up to 2147483648.
N1.label: N1 compiler and SIMD dependence established

symptoms_visible: After updating the Intel-compiler build to NumPy 1.26.4, np.any still returns True for all-False arrays of length 64 or greater.
Disabling AVX512_SKX still makes the result correct, but my 50-call benchmark takes 7.002 seconds instead of 1.488 seconds.
N2_x.label: N2_x NumPy update aftermath

symptoms_visible: After rebuilding Python and NumPy with Intel oneAPI 2022.2.1, the all-False length-64 test still returns True with AVX512_SKX enabled and returns False when AVX512_SKX is disabled.
N3_x.label: N3_x older Intel Classic compiler aftermath

symptoms_visible: My Intel LLVM icx build has AVX512 enabled and returns False for the original all-False test, but the benchmark takes about 9 seconds.
The comparable Intel Classic icc build takes about 2 seconds but returns the wrong result in the original test.
N4.label: N4 Intel LLVM and Classic builds compared

symptoms_visible: The Intel LLVM build returns the correct False result with AVX512 enabled, although it is slower; the Intel Classic build still produces the incorrect True result unless AVX512_SKX is disabled.
N_terminal.label: terminal compiler defect diagnosed without final NumPy-side fix confirmation

question_patterns: Where did this NumPy installation come from, and which compiler was used to build it?
Is this an official wheel or a source build, and was it built with GCC or an Intel compiler?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I compiled NumPy from source because I wanted to link it to Intel MKL, and I used the Intel compiler.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: This is an unmodified official pip wheel built with GCC, and I can reproduce it on several ordinary x86_64 machines.
It is still a source build using Intel Compiler Classic, but linked to a different MKL installation.

question_patterns: Can you disable individual high-end CPU features at runtime and rerun the length-64 test?
Please test the reduction while excluding SIMD features one at a time and report the exact setting and output.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I tried disabling different CPU features. With export NPY_DISABLE_CPU_FEATURES="AVX512_SKX", the problem goes away. I tested all-False arrays up to length 2147483648, and np.any still returned False.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The result remains True at length 64 regardless of which CPU feature I disable, including when all optional SIMD dispatch is disabled.
Disabling the same feature makes the length-64 and length-65 tests return False, but I did not test very large arrays.

edges.comment: Thread c3-c6, reporter's system: participant3 asked about installation source and CPU-feature exclusions; the reporter disclosed the Intel source build and reported the raw AVX512_SKX-disabled test results.

solution.intent: Upgrade from NumPy 1.26.2 to 1.26.4 in case a related reduction or SIMD fix was already included.
solution.concrete_example: Build and install NumPy 1.26.4 with the same compiler setup, then rerun the 63- and 64-element tests.

edges.comment: Thread c3 and c8-c13, reporter's system: the suggested 1.26.4 update was installed and retained, but the same boundary failure remained. The reporter also re-established the runtime workaround and measured its slowdown.

solution.intent: Rebuild with an older Intel oneAPI Compiler Classic release to determine whether the behavior is confined to the initially used compiler version.
solution.concrete_example: Recompile Python and NumPy with Intel oneAPI 2022.2.1 and repeat the all-False reduction test with the same SIMD configuration.

edges.comment: Thread c15-c16, reporter's primary system: the reporter rebuilt Python and NumPy with oneAPI 2022.2.1. This persistent compiler-version change did not correct the result, and the same CPU-feature workaround remained effective.

solution.intent: Rebuild NumPy with the Intel LLVM compiler rather than Intel Compiler Classic, retain AVX512 support, and compare correctness and performance.
solution.concrete_example: Build with icx using the reporter's optimized flags, confirm that AVX512 remains available, and rerun both the length-64 correctness test and the large-array timing test.

edges.comment: Thread c33-c37, reporter's system: participant4 documented an Intel LLVM build route, and the reporter ultimately retained an icx-built NumPy. The reporter's own comparison showed correct output with icx and incorrect output with icc, while also recording the performance difference.

solution.intent: Diagnose the failure as an Intel Compiler Classic optimizer defect in the AVX512_SKX boolean-reduction path, not a NumPy-version or MKL semantic error; avoid the affected Classic-generated path by using Intel LLVM or temporarily disabling AVX512_SKX, and require a retest before claiming any future NumPy-side workaround is resolved.
solution.concrete_example: The Intel Compiler Classic optimizer miscompiles the AVX512 mask logic used by this reduction. Use an icx-built NumPy for correct AVX512-enabled behavior, or keep NPY_DISABLE_CPU_FEATURES="AVX512_SKX" as a temporary slower workaround. Do not claim that upgrading NumPy alone fixes it, and verify any eventual NumPy-side compiler workaround on the affected system.
solution.inference_hint: Participant6's final analysis established the compiler mechanism: comparing the scalar result of _cvtmask64_u64 with -1 under Intel Compiler Classic can make the optimizer duplicate the last zmm comparison on ymm and XOR the two masks. The minimal NumPy SIMD reproducer returning 1 for an all-zero vector and the assembly-level explanation are maintainer-produced diagnosis, not facts supplied by the reporter.

edges.comment: Thread c38, participant6's analysis of the reporter's issue: Intel Compiler Classic was confirmed as the source across versions, while Intel LLVM did not exhibit the defect. No affected-user comment follows this diagnosis confirming a final NumPy-side patch, so the terminal state records an accepted diagnosis and tested workarounds without marking the reporter fully resolved.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the final accepted root cause as an Intel Compiler Classic optimizer bug in the AVX512_SKX mask/reduction path, rather than a general np.any defect, an MKL computation error, or a NumPy 1.26.2-only regression.

The diagnosis must be grounded in the collected evidence: disabling AVX512_SKX restores correct output, NumPy 1.26.4 and an older Intel Classic compiler still fail, and an AVX512-enabled Intel LLVM build returns the correct result.
Must not present upgrading to NumPy 1.26.4 or downgrading to an older Intel Compiler Classic release as the fix; both were tried on the reporter's system and retained the incorrect result.
A practical workaround may use an Intel LLVM icx build or disable AVX512_SKX, but it must acknowledge the reporter's measured performance penalty rather than claiming an equivalent optimized fix.

Must not declare a NumPy-side fix fully resolved without asking the affected user to verify a rebuilt or patched NumPy on the affected system; the thread ends after the maintainer's compiler diagnosis without such a follow-up confirmation.

persona_hint.experience_level: Highly technical HPC and scientific-computing user who builds Python and NumPy from source, links against Intel MKL, edits compiler configuration, compares Intel compiler generations, inspects SIMD dispatch, and runs large-array benchmarks.
persona_hint.communication_style: Detailed, persistent, and evidence-driven. Provides exact commands, flags, build logs, configuration output, and timing results; asks practical follow-up questions when build-system guidance is unclear and explicitly weighs correctness against performance.
